reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: The most common cause of congenital lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, caused by obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra
Many cases are suspected antenatally from bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick-walled distended bladder, a dilated posterior urethra (keyhole sign), and oligohydramnios
Severe early obstruction and oligohydramnios can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia, which may be the immediate life-threatening problem at birth
Postnatal presentation ranges from a palpable bladder, poor urinary stream, and straining to urosepsis or failure to thrive, and older boys may present with voiding difficulty or incontinence
The voiding cystourethrogram is the key diagnostic study, showing a dilated posterior urethra, bladder trabeculation, and often vesicoureteric reflux
Initial management is bladder decompression with a catheter, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and treatment of infection before definitive intervention
Definitive treatment is endoscopic ablation of the valves, with temporary urinary diversion (vesicostomy) reserved for selected infants
Long-term follow-up is essential because bladder dysfunction and progressive renal impairment can persist or evolve even after successful valve ablation
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing tissue folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of males that impede bladder emptying from early in fetal life. The resulting high-pressure obstruction causes bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation, vesicoureteric reflux, and back-pressure that dilates the ureters and damages the developing kidneys, producing dysplasia and impaired concentrating ability. Reduced fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios, which in turn impairs lung development and can result in pulmonary hypoplasia. The renal and bladder damage sustained in utero often determines lifelong outcome.
additionalInvestigations: Voiding cystourethrogram to demonstrate the valves and assess reflux and bladder morphology
Renal and bladder ultrasound to evaluate hydronephrosis and bladder wall thickness
Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine to assess renal function (interpreted after the first days of life)
Cystoscopy for direct visualisation and treatment of the valves
Isotope renography to assess differential renal function and drainage
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to oligohydramnios, which is immediately life-threatening
Urosepsis in an infant with obstruction requiring urgent decompression and antibiotics
Acute kidney injury with electrolyte disturbance and rising creatinine
Progressive deterioration in renal function or bladder function despite valve ablation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends largely on the degree of irreversible renal dysplasia established in utero. Many boys do well after valve ablation, but a significant proportion develop chronic kidney disease and bladder dysfunction, and some progress to end-stage renal failure requiring transplantation. Early nadir creatinine after treatment is a useful prognostic indicator.
pitfalls: Attributing an antenatal keyhole bladder or bilateral hydronephrosis to a benign cause and delaying evaluation
Interpreting neonatal creatinine in the first day or two as the baby's true renal function rather than the mother's
Assuming valve ablation cures the child and neglecting long-term renal and bladder surveillance
Overlooking bladder dysfunction as an ongoing cause of upper tract deterioration
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Stabilise the newborn first with bladder decompression via a urethral catheter, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and treatment of any infection
Provide neonatal respiratory support for pulmonary hypoplasia, which may be the immediate life-threatening problem at birth
Perform definitive endoscopic valve ablation once the infant is stable, with a temporary vesicostomy as an alternative in the very small or unstable baby
Institute long-term management of the resulting valve-bladder dysfunction with anticholinergics, timed or double voiding and clean intermittent catheterisation where needed

Provide nephrology surveillance of renal function and growth, managing chronic kidney disease with attention to fluid, electrolytes, acidosis and nutrition, and plan for dialysis or transplantation if end-stage failure develops
Monitor for and treat urinary tract infections and vesicoureteric reflux, with antibiotic prophylaxis where indicated
Offer antenatal counselling, delivery planning and family support given the guarded renal prognosis
